item.title: Biman to purchase 10 Airbus aircraft; deal expected in October
item.description:
Shortly after signing an agreement with Boeing to purchase 25 aircraft, the government is set to buy 10 more aircraft from European aircraft manufacturer Airbus for Biman Bangladesh Airlines.
“We are buying 10 Airbus aircraft. Inshallah, the agreement will be signed in October,” Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat announced on Tuesday at a press briefing held at the Secretariat.
Earlier, Bangladesh signed an agreement with Boeing to purchase 25 aircraft, Millat said, clarifying that signing the agreement does not mean the aircraft will arrive in Bangladesh immediately.
“Under the agreement, the first Boeing aircraft is scheduled to arrive in 2031. However, Bangladesh has requested Boeing to deliver at least one aircraft by 2027-28. 25 Boeing aircraft will be delivered in phases through 2035-37,” the minister said.
He said payment would be made after each aircraft is delivered, meaning Bangladesh will not have to pay the full amount upfront.
“Now, we don't have to pay any money. We are giving a guarantee that they will provide the aircraft one by one, and then we will pay. Hopefully, we will be able to pay this money from the earnings of this fleet,” he said.
The minister said the 25 Boeing aircraft will cost around $6.4 billion in total.
The previous agreement for 14 Boeing aircraft was worth $3.7 billion, while the newly added 11 aircraft will cost around $2.7 billion, he said.
The prices of the 11 new Boeing aircraft were set in line with the earlier agreement, Millat added.
As it will take several years for the newly purchased aircraft to be delivered, the government has taken an initiative to lease at least 10 aircraft to expand Biman’s fleet in the meantime, said the minister.
“We will lease at least 10 aircraft until the new planes arrive,” he said.
The leasing process is underway, Millat said, adding that a committee headed by the finance secretary has been formed with representatives of all relevant stakeholders.
He said two more members have been proposed to ensure that the aircraft leasing process is completed transparently.
The minister said the government wants to expand Biman’s fleet through leasing and develop the country’s aviation sector.
Asked whether the Boeing purchase was aimed at pleasing the United States, the minister said the decision on which country to purchase aircraft from is entirely Bangladesh's own.
He said the government is considering which aircraft would be suitable for Bangladesh, where they could be purchased most profitably and how many aircraft should be bought in the country's interest.
“What we should think about is how Bangladesh will benefit, where we can buy profitably, and from whom and how many we should buy to benefit the country,” he said.
“We all — not just me, but also those who are taking my photo or recording what I say — should think that we put Bangladesh first,” he added.
The minister said it was not his concern whether a “level playing field” has been created for any other country.
Aircraft would be purchased from whichever source would be most beneficial for Bangladesh's aviation sector, he said.

item.title: Iftekharuzzaman: Interim govt failed, current govt heading same way
item.description:
The interim government failed to form the Information Commission, and the current government is heading in the same direction, Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) Executive Director Dr Iftekharuzzaman has said.
“The interim government failed to form the commission. Many of those who were in the government were our friends. We held their hands and urged them to form the commission. They failed. The current government has completed seven months and is heading in the same direction,” he said.
Iftekharuzzaman made the remarks at a conference in Dhaka on Tuesday, marking International Right To Know Day 2026.
Dr Iftekharuzzaman: “The government has been extremely eager to form the commission but has failed, and is heading towards creating this world record. It is extremely embarrassing. This is a violation of the law. When ordinary people violate the law, we are held accountable. What happens when the government violates the law?”
“The only judgment for the government is the people’s trust. If it loses that trust, it is reflected in different ways. History reminds everyone of that,” he also said.
Iftekharuzzaman said he hoped the commission would be genuinely independent and impartial.
“We want to remain hopeful that the commission will be truly independent and capable of working impartially,” he said.
“Although the track record does not give me much reason for optimism, I want to see what kind of commission is actually formed,” he added.
He said forming the commission was a major challenge for the government.
“It is a major challenge for the government to give the people a commission that will increase their confidence in the Information Commission and, through that, increase their confidence in the government,” he said.
Iftekharuzzaman also criticized what he described as the politicization of institutions.
“Even after the current government took responsibility, we have seen politicization in these kinds of institutions,” he said.
He said the Information Commission had previously been operated by party cadres and warned against a repeat of the same situation.
“In the past, the Information Commission was operated by party cadres and the doors were closed to us. If the same situation happens again, or even if something similar happens, I do not want to rule out that possibility,” he said.
He said the government appeared to be conflating the RTI law with measures aimed at addressing misinformation.
“Now the government is trying, intentionally or unintentionally, to mix up the issue of the Information Commission and amendments to the Right to Information Act with misinformation,” he said.
“There is nowhere in the world where you mix up the right to information with misinformation, disinformation or false information. You make separate laws to regulate misinformation and false information. But the right to information and misinformation are completely different things,” he said.
The remarks came as the findings of the Bangladesh Right to Information National Survey 2026, titled Reality Check and Pathways for Breakthrough, were presented at the event.
The survey was conducted by Principal Investigator Dr Ananya Raihan and was based on responses from 3,200 citizens, 100 designated officers, 20 appellate authorities, 15 focus group discussions and an analysis of 100 Information Commission decisions from 2018 to 2024.
Participants at a conference to mark International Right To Know Day 2026 in Dhaka on Tuesday, September 29, 2026. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
The survey found that 72.4% of citizens need government or institutional information, up from 68.3% in 2019.
Citizens most frequently sought information on employment, development projects, social safety-net programs, education, government initiatives, agriculture and allocation of public funds.
Overall awareness of the RTI Act increased from 7.7% in 2019 to 10.5% in 2025.
However, knowledge of the procedures for exercising the right remains low.
Among citizens who had heard of the RTI law, 69.5% knew only the name of the law. Only 18% knew what information they could request, while 9.3% knew the legal timeframe for receiving information, down from 16.3% in 2019. Only 8.5% knew how to submit an application.
There was also considerable confusion over where complaints should be filed when information is denied. While 44.5% believed a union parishad chairman handled complaints, only 19.9% correctly identified the Information Commission.
Social media has become an increasingly important source of awareness, rising from 11% in 2019 to 33.3%. Television’s share declined from 47.7% to 25.2%.
The proportion of aware citizens who had filed RTI applications increased from 2.8% to 4.6%.
The proportion receiving information within the prescribed timeframe rose from 13.2% to 48.5%. However, the rate of applicants receiving acknowledgement fell from 75.4% to 43.8%, while overall positive experiences declined from 55.8% to 48.5%.
The survey also found a major shift in the institutions citizens approached for information. Applications to the Election Commission rose nearly eightfold, from 3.3% to 24.8%, while applications to union parishads declined from 27.9% to 14.2%.
According to the survey, 86% of complaints filed with the Information Commission resulted from inactivity by appellate authorities or unreasonable rejection of applications.
In 63% of cases, it took more than 30 days for complaints to be admitted for hearing.
The survey found that 23% of positive decisions by the Information Commission were never implemented, while 15% of cases required a second complaint because the decisions were not followed.
The survey identified institutional harassment and fear of retaliation as major barriers to using the RTI law.
Fifty-nine percent of citizens said women face greater barriers when seeking information. Administrative negligence was identified as a major obstacle for women by 32.7% of respondents, while 14.1% cited direct harassment.
BLAST Honorary Executive Director Barrister Sara Hossain said fear was one of the major reasons people did not use the RTI law.
“People think that if they ask a question, they may face trouble again. In a country where many people do not seek legal remedies even after suffering injustice because they fear that their rights may be violated again, or that they themselves could be made the accused, it is understandable that people would be afraid to raise questions through the RTI law,” she said.
She said marginalised, poor and powerless people were particularly unable to use the law.
“The question is how we can change this situation,” she said.
Hossain urged the authorities to make the Information Commission functional without waiting for a perfect reform process.
“Whatever shortcomings there may be in the Information Commission, we should now try to make it functional. Once the commission starts working, opportunities for reform will emerge through its work. But if we wait for a ‘perfect’ reform, the situation we are going through cannot continue indefinitely,” she said.
She noted that two and a half years had already passed and said the current situation could not continue indefinitely.
EU Delegation First Counsellor Kamila Partyka said the survey highlighted a significant gap between citizens’ need for information and their awareness of the RTI framework.
“More than 72% of citizens surveyed say they need or expect to need information, while only slightly over 10% are aware of the RTI framework. So, this is a huge gap that exists, and closing this gap is not only about increasing awareness. It is also about ensuring that information is accessible, timely, usable, and that institutions are equipped to provide it,” she said.
“Access to information is a fundamental element of transparent, accountable and participatory governance. It enables citizens to understand decisions that affect their lives, access public services, participate meaningfully in public affairs and hold institutions accountable,” she said.
MJF Executive Director Shaheen Anam said the RTI Act, enacted in 2009 following a campaign involving civil society, journalists, human rights activists and other organizations, was intended to strengthen good governance and government accountability.
“The purpose was to ensure good governance, accountability of the government and openness by moving away from a culture of secrecy. We all are taxpayers. This law has given us the right to question the government,” she said.
“The purpose was for every citizen to be able to seek information freely and without fear. How much we have achieved that purpose and how much we have not, you will judge,” she added.
The survey found that 91.6% of citizens considered the RTI Act a “very good law”, while 56% believed it could improve the quality of public services.
It recommended proactive disclosure of information on land, budgets and public services, legal protection for information seekers against retaliation, amendments to address gaps in the 2009 RTI Act and a digital “Citizen Connect” platform for submitting and tracking applications.

item.title: 6 more dengue deaths reported in 24hrs, 1,942 hospitalized
item.description:
Six more people died of dengue and 1,942 new patients were hospitalized across the country in the 24 hours until 8am on Tuesday.
With the latest fatalities, the dengue death toll has risen to 239 in the country this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Among the deaths, three each died in Rajshahi division, while one each died in Dhaka division, Dhaka South City Corporation and Dhaka North City Corporation.
Of the total deaths recorded this year, 47.1% were men and 52.9% were women.
Since January 1 this year, a total of 77,672 dengue patients were admitted to hospitals across the country. Of them, 72,008 have recovered.
According to the DGHS report, so far 69 people have died in Dhaka South City Corporation till September 28 this year, while 45 in Khulna division, 29 in Dhaka North City Corporation, 23 in Chittagong division, 20 in Mymensingh division, 18 in Barisal division, 15 in Dhaka division, 14 in Rajshahi division, five in Rangpur and one in Sylhet divisions.

item.title: Bangladesh move to semi-final after rain ruins match against Malaysia
item.description:
Bangladesh secured a spot in the men's cricket semi-finals of the 2026 Asian Games after heavy rain washed out their quarterfinal against Malaysia without a ball being bowled today.
The match was abandoned before the toss as persistent rain continued to disrupt the cricket schedule at Korogi Sports Park in Nagoya, Japan.
Bangladesh secured their place in the last four based on their higher T20I ranking, while Malaysia eliminated under the tournament's rules for rain-affected matches.
All four men's cricket quarterfinals were abandoned because of rain, with no play possible in the Bangladesh-Malaysia and Sri Lanka-Nepal matches today.
Bangladesh, led by Liton Das, will face Pakistan in the semifinal on October 1. India will meet Sri Lanka in the other semifinal on the same day.
The weather could again play a decisive role. If the Bangladesh-Pakistan semifinal is abandoned without play, Pakistan would advance to the final because of its higher ranking.
The repeated washouts have raised concerns over the possibility of further disruption to the Asian Games cricket schedule.

item.title: UN: 8.3m refugees at risk due to ‘severe’ funding cuts
item.description:
Nearly 8.3 million refugees and other forcibly displaced people face losing vital assistance from UNHCR, the UN’s refugee agency warned Tuesday, as protection services crumble due to “severe” funding cuts.
“UNHCR’s ability to protect and assist refugees, internally displaced people (IDPs) and stateless people is being eroded by a sustained and worsening funding shortfall,” the agency said in a report detailing the human cost of budget cuts.
The agency said its available funding had fallen from $5.2 billion in 2024 to $3.9 billion in 2025, while the number of people it is mandated to protect is hovering around historically high levels.
UNHCR said it needed $8.5 billion this year to protect refugees, but by the end of July had received only 32% of that amount ($2.7 billion).
This means nearly 8.3 million forcibly displaced people are “at risk of losing access to UNHCR assistance,” the agency said.
“Continued severe funding cuts are pushing refugee support and protection structures towards breaking point in the world’s main displacement situations,” it added.
UNHCR said it had undertaken reforms and prioritization measures to protect its most critical work -- but said the scale and persistence of the shortfall meant that even its highest-priority work was now being affected.
“Protection cannot be reduced indefinitely without systems collapsing,” said Dominique Hyde, UNHCR’s external relations chief.
“Below a certain threshold, services do not simply reach fewer people; they can stop functioning altogether, leaving those most at risk without the protection they need.”
The agency said that in Chad, 319,000 refugees faced registration delays, leaving them without the documentation to access services, while around 233,000 children could lose child protection services.
In Ethiopia, child protection coverage in some areas has diminished by up to 85%.
And in Sudan, tens of thousands of survivors of sexual violence and children at serious risk could lose access to critical protection services, the agency warned.
When registration stops or child protection services disappear, “the very risks that people fled -- violence, exploitation and abuse -- reappear in displacement,” warned Hyde.
Some 117.8 million people worldwide were forcibly displaced from their homes at the end of 2025, according to UNHCR -- down from 2024’s record 123.2 million.
Of those 117.8 million, 35.6 million were refugees under UNHCR’s mandate, with two-thirds coming from Venezuela, Ukraine, Syria, Afghanistan and Sudan.
UNHCR shed nearly 5,000 jobs in 2025 -- more than a quarter of its workforce. The United States -- traditionally the world’s top donor -- has heavily slashed foreign aid, while other major donors have been tightening their belts.
The Geneva-based agency said funding cuts were undermining its efforts to help people move away from reliance on aid.
In Iraq, up to 350,000 refugees and asylum seekers risk losing access to economic inclusion opportunities, it said.
And when people return to their home countries -- whether voluntarily or under duress -- help is also drying up, said UNHCR.
In Syria, 162,500 vulnerable IDPs and returned refugees will not receive initial financial assistance unless funding is received quickly, reducing their ability to rebuild their lives, the agency said.

item.title: Summer, Still
item.description:
I keep expecting tomorrow
to remember how July behaved,
to leave the windows open
past the hour they should be closed.
I keep expecting the peaches
to bruise from sweetness alone,
the sunlight to believe in forever,
the evenings to arrive slowly enough
that conversation forgets where it meant to end.
These were days
that asked nothing of me
except to stay.
I mistook that for ordinary.
I thought every season
would know how to linger.
Now the days have become careful again.
Still, some evenings hesitate
at the edge of night,
as though daylight
has forgotten
how to say goodbye.
I keep expecting August
to inherit July's manners
to stay past dark,
to call my name,
and say,
not yet.
Summer, still.
Nafisa Afreen Megha is an aspiring writer. Her work consists of her individual thoughts, reflections on womanhood, and critiques of societal norms.

item.title: Govt ‘saddened and embarrassed’ by vandalism at Radda Health Centre
item.description:
Prime Minister’s Adviser on Information and Broadcasting Dr Zahed Ur Rahman has said the government is “saddened and embarrassed” by the vandalism at the Radda MCH-FP Centre in Mirpur and allegations of involvement by members of the ruling party.
“The government is saddened whenever the rights of any citizen are violated, any facility is vandalised, or an individual is attacked. Ensuring citizens’ safety is the government’s responsibility, so such incidents cause embarrassment to the government,” he said.
He made the remarks at the Department of Information’s conference room at the Secretariat on Tuesday afternoon during a weekly briefing on the progress of government activities. He later responded to questions from journalists.
Asked what action would be taken if members of the ruling party were found to be involved, Zahed said: “Whoever is found to be linked to the incident through the investigation will be brought to justice.”
He said media investigations were important, but the police investigation would ultimately form the basis of the charge sheet.
“If the police confirm anyone’s involvement during the investigation, action will be taken against them as well,” he said.
Zahed said such incidents have a serious impact on the public.
“The state’s primary duty is to prevent crime. Once a crime has occurred, it is also crucial to ensure swift justice so that similar incidents do not happen in the future,” he said.

item.title: Man sentenced to death for raping 13-year-old stepdaughter in Dhaka
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Tuesday sentenced a 43-year-old man to death and fined him Tk 5 lakh for raping his 13-year-old step-daughter in the capital’s Kamrangirchar area.
Judge Masrur Salekin of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal, also a district and sessions judge, pronounced the verdict on September 29. Bench Assistant Pankaj Peter Gomes confirmed the matter.
According to the case statement, the victim was a seventh-grade student who lived with the accused, her mother’s second husband.
On August 28, 2023, the accused allegedly raped the girl at their home in Nabinagar, Kamrangirchar, when no one else was present. He later raped her several times, threatening to kill her. The girl became pregnant and subsequently gave birth to a child.
The victim’s mother filed a case under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act with Kamrangirchar Police Station on the same day.
After completing the investigation, police submitted a charge sheet against the accused on January 23, 2025. The tribunal framed charges on August 24, 2025, and commenced the trial.
During the trial, the court recorded testimony from six prosecution witnesses. After examining the evidence and hearing arguments, the court found the accused guilty and sentenced him to death, along with a fine of Tk 5 lakh.
Under Section 9(1) of the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act, 2000, the court ordered that the convict be hanged by the neck until death.
The fine will be paid to the victim or her legal guardian. If the amount is not paid within the stipulated period, the court ordered that it be recovered by auctioning the convict’s movable or immovable property.
In its observations, the court said Section 9(1) provides two sentencing options for rape: the death penalty or life imprisonment with hard labour.
The court observed that Jamal Hossain had raped a 13-year-old child and that ensuring appropriate punishment for such an offence was its responsibility.
Citing a decision of the Supreme Court’s Appellate Division, the court said the crime was committed not only against the victim but also against the society to which she belongs.

item.title: IGP: Criminals to face action regardless of political affiliation
item.description:
Inspector General of Police Md Ali Hossain Fakir has directed police to take legal action against drug dealers, criminals and extortionists regardless of their political affiliation.
“There is no scope to consider an offender’s political affiliation. The only identity of a criminal is that he is a criminal,” he said.
He also instructed field-level officers to take appropriate legal action against juvenile offenders.
The IGP gave the directives at the monthly crime review meeting for August 2026 at Police Headquarters on Tuesday morning.
He said the police’s “zero tolerance” policy against drugs would continue and directed officers to take measures to prevent drug trafficking and the spread of narcotics.
He also stressed community policing and greater public participation in preventing drug-related crimes.
The IGP instructed field-level officers to ensure adequate security for the upcoming Durga Puja celebrations and take measures to prevent rumours and misinformation.
The meeting was chaired by Additional IGP (Crime and Operations) Md Sayedur Rahman.
Regarding teen gangs, the IGP directed officers to gather information on the gangs, investigate whether influential individuals were operating behind them and take legal action accordingly.

item.title: Can US sanctions ground Iran’s aviation industry?
item.description:
US sanctions are pushing Iran’s weakened aviation sector toward deeper isolation, making international travel less predictable and raising new risks for trade and cargo.
Earlier in September as part of “Operation Economic Outcast,” the US Treasury Department targeted Iran’s aviation sector, including Iranian airlines and companies providing ground handling, ticketing or airport support, which face secondary sanctions and may lose access to the US financial system.
The United States cannot directly order foreign airports to reject Iranian aircraft. But the threat of secondary sanctions can make servicing them too risky for airports, fuel suppliers and aviation companies.
For Tehran, the aviation sanctions are another layer of Washington’s broader pressure campaign, alongside restrictions on banking, shipping, insurance and trade.
Washington argues that Iranian airlines have served not only civilian passengers but also military and security networks.
For example, Mahan Air has been accused of supporting the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and helping transport personnel and equipment.
The issue has also been debated inside Iran. Former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif said in a 2021 interview that Qassem Soleimani had used civilian aircraft to move forces and equipment to Syria.
For Washington, such links help justify targeting aviation networks. For ordinary travelers, however, the immediate result is canceled flights and fewer ways to leave or return to the country.
Iranian flights to Baghdad and Muscat have been suspended or canceled, while Azerbaijan and Georgia also stopped accepting flights operated by Iranian carriers. An Iranian travel agency told DW anonymously, for safety reasons, that routes to Oman, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Georgia had been seriously disrupted.
On September 24, Turkmenistan refused permission for an Iranian aircraft flying from Tehran to Dushanbe to cross its airspace, forcing the plane to return to Iran.
Turkey, Armenia and China have not announced blanket restrictions, the agency said, but passengers were increasingly reluctant to buy tickets because even a confirmed booking did not guarantee departure.
One passenger told DW that agencies would still sell him a ticket but could not guarantee the flight would actually operate.
As part of the sanctions package, the US also suspended the “J-1” general license, which had allowed certain non-Iranian aircraft to make temporary stops in Iran under specific conditions, including that control of the aircraft remained with the foreign operator and that the stay did not exceed permitted limits.
Many commercial aircraft contain US-made parts or technology, meaning operations involving Iran can fall under US sanctions rules.
The suspension of J-1 has increased the legal and financial risks for airlines, airports, fuel suppliers, ground-handling companies and other service providers, who now must calculate the risk of secondary sanctions.
With air connections increasingly uncertain, more passengers are turning to land crossings.
One traveler whose flight was canceled told DW that he traveled overland from Iran to Turkey before continuing to Istanbul by air.
“The border was very crowded. A lot of people were trying to leave because they were worried the routes might close,” he told DW anonymously.
For families, older people, students and patients, however, crossing a land border and continuing by road and air can be far more difficult than taking a direct flight. Costs also rise quickly as passengers add road transport, accommodation and additional flights to journeys that previously required a single ticket.
Also affected is air freight, which is important for urgent or sensitive goods, including some medicines, medical equipment, industrial parts and laboratory samples.
That has become more significant as Iran simultaneously faces severe restrictions on maritime trade.
Iranian aviation already faced structural problems before the latest sanctions.
Transport Minister Farzaneh Sadegh previously acknowledged that some flights operate without radar guidance, leaving pilots with greater responsibility for navigation.
An ageing fleet, difficulties obtaining spare parts, years of sanctions and fewer operational aircraft have all put pressure on airlines.
When passengers must also consider destination airports refusing services, lengthy delays or flights being canceled without warning, buying a ticket becomes a calculation of risk.
Alireza Salavati, political economy analyst and managing director of the London-based Middle East Analytica, said that the loss of air links will be unlikely to cause a large, immediate hit to Iran’s GDP.
“Iran’s aviation sector is small by regional standards. Unlike Turkey or the UAE, the country is not a major international hub, and its commercial fleet is limited. Officials said in July that roughly 150 aircraft were in the operational pool, with only about half of them operational at any given time,” Salavati told DW.
“The damage is more apparent in connectivity. For a heavily sanctioned economy, flights still matter for business, the diaspora, students, specialist workers and medical treatment abroad. For patients, a once-direct journey can become a detour through a third country, with extra travel, accommodation and sometimes visa costs. Time can matter as much as money,” Salavati added.
Foreign airlines had already sharply reduced services to Iran before the latest measures.
Many passengers relied on Iranian carriers to reach regional hubs such as Istanbul, Muscat, Baghdad or Yerevan, then continued with foreign airlines.
If those first connections disappear, Iran’s international aviation network could increasingly be reduced to a handful of routes that remain politically and commercially viable.
The development also comes as Iran faces restrictions at sea. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, higher insurance and freight costs and pressure on southern ports had already made imports and exports more difficult.
If maritime trade becomes more expensive while air links also contract, Iran will become increasingly dependent on land borders and indirect routes through neighboring states.

item.title: Child injured in gunfight between two groups in Sajek
item.description:
A nine-year-old girl was injured in an exchange of gunfire between armed groups backed by the UPDF (Prasit) and JSS (Santu Larma) in Sajek of Rangamati’s Baghaichari upazila on Tuesday.
The incident took place around 8am in the Chailyatali area of Sajek.
According to local sources, the two groups exchanged several hundred rounds of gunfire over establishing control in the area.
Sanjita Tripura, a resident of Chailyatali, was hit by a bullet in her left hand during the exchange.
The bullet was later removed from her hand, and she is currently in stable condition, police said.
Sajek police station Officer-in-Charge Tofail Ahmed said the two groups exchanged gunfire in the morning over establishing control in the area.
He said the child was injured in her left hand during the shooting and that the bullet had been removed. She is currently in stable condition.
