Southeast Bank unveils MFS platform TeleCash
item.description:
With a commitment to expanding financial inclusion and building a cashless or digital economy in Bangladesh, mobile financial services (MFS) provider TeleCash Limited has commenced its commercial operations.
A subsidiary of Southeast Bank PLC, TeleCash Limited received the final approval from Bangladesh Bank on September 24, to commence its commercial services.
To mark this achievement, an inauguration ceremony was held on September 29, at the head office of Southeast Bank PLC in Dhaka.
The inauguration ceremony was graced by MA Kashem, chairman and founder chairman of Southeast Bank PLC and former president of FBCCI, as chief guest.
Nasir Uddin Ahmed, chairman of the board of directors of TeleCash Limited, attended the ceremony as special guest.
Also present at the event were Md Khalid Mahmud Khan, managing director & CEO of Southeast Bank PLC, and AKM Monirul Islam, acting managing director of TeleCash Limited, along with members of the boards of directors and senior officials of both organizations.
MA Kashem, chairman of Southeast Bank PLC, said: “The commencement of TeleCash Limited’s journey is a landmark step towards strengthening financial inclusion in Bangladesh and taking digital financial services to a new height. As the parent bank, Southeast Bank is committed to providing TeleCash with the necessary strategic support and guidance so that it can deliver safe, convenient and innovative financial solutions to the people.”
Nasir Uddin Ahmed, chairman of TeleCash Limited, said: “The formal launch of TeleCash marks an important milestone in our commitment to advancing digital financial services in the country. By leveraging the experience and support of Southeast Bank, we are committed to building a secure, reliable and customer-centric MFS platform that will contribute meaningfully to the sustainable growth of the country’s digital economy.”
AKM Monirul Islam, acting managing director of TeleCash Limited, outlined the company’s business strategy and objectives, stating: “TeleCash does not aspire to be merely another MFS brand in the market; rather, we aim to build a trusted platform by combining technological excellence, risk-conscious operations and sound corporate governance.”

item.title: ADB, Modern Syntex sign $50m loan to expand polyester chips production
item.description:
The Asian Development Bank (ADB) and Modern Syntex Limited (MSL) on Tuesday signed a $50 million loan for the Modern Energy-Efficient Polyester Chips Manufacturing Project in Bangladesh.
The financing will support MSL's expansion of polyester chips production capacity from 107 tonnes to 407 tonnes per day and refinance short-term local working capital loans.
The expanded facility will produce high intrinsic viscosity polyester chips used in higher-value textile and apparel products.
"Bangladesh's textile and ready-made garment industry is a key driver of the economy, but it continues to rely heavily on imported synthetic inputs," said ADB country director for Bangladesh Qingfeng Zhang.
"ADB's long-term financing will help MSL expand efficient domestic production, deepen backward linkages, strengthen supply chains, and support higher-value textile manufacturing.
The project will also contribute to the development of the Mirsarai Economic Zone and support Bangladesh's efforts to attract investment, create jobs, and enhance economic competitiveness."
The project will introduce energy-efficient machinery, expected to save about 4,840 megawatt-hours of electricity and reduce about 2,222 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions each year.
It will also help MSL pursue Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (Leed) Platinum certification for its building and factory.
The project is expected to strengthen Bangladesh's textile value chain by increasing domestic supply of polyester chips, reducing reliance on imports, shortening lead times, and improving efficiency for textile manufacturers.
It will also create about 100 new jobs and promote greater participation of women through inclusive recruitment practices.
“We greatly value ADB’s support as it enables MSL to significantly expand polyester chips production, strengthen local supply chains, and reduce dependence on imported inputs,” said MSL managing director Abu Sufian Chowdhury.
“By investing in advanced energy-efficient technology, we are improving our competitiveness while supporting a more sustainable textile industry. We believe this project will create long-term value for our customers, the manufacturing sector, and the broader economy.”
MSL is part of TK Group and operates Bangladesh's first continuous polymerization facility, strategically located in the Mirsarai Economic Zone in Chittagong, close to major port and logistics infrastructure.
The company manufactures polyester chips, synthetic yarn, and fiber, primarily for domestic textile manufacturers.

item.title: Labaid celebrates World Heart Day
item.description:
Marking World Heart Day with the theme “Don’t Miss a beat” Labaid Cardiac Hospital has organized a day-long “Free Cardiac Consultation” program.
Under this initiative, visitors to the hospital, patients’ relatives, and general public are being given the opportunity to learn about their heart health.
They can also seek advice from specialist physicians when necessary.
As part of the World Heart Day observance, a seminar on heart disease and its prevention was organized at the hospital.
Dr Md Mohasin Uddin presented a keynote on the subject at the seminar.
Prominent cardiologists from across the country attended the event.
Dr Abduz Zaher chaired the seminar.
The panel of experts included Prof Dr Baren Chakraborty, Dr Md Lokman Hossain, Dr Arun Kumar Sharma, Dr S Mokaddas Hossain (Sadi), and Dr Nur Mohammad.
Dr Mahbubur Rahman moderated the event.
The hospital’s medical directors and other senior officials were also present.
Earlier in the morning, a colorful rally was organized to mark World Heart Day.
The rally began at Labaid Cardiac Hospital, proceeded through Green Road and Mirpur Road, and returned to Labaid Cardiac Hospital, where it concluded.
The rally was inaugurated by Ahmed Dawood, chief executive officer of Labaid Hospital.
Senior consultants, medical directors, senior officials, and large number of nurses and healthcare workers attended the rally.
Meanwhile, on the occasion of World Heart Day 2026, a “Special cardiac screening package” has begun at Labaid Cardiac Hospital, the country’s first hospital to receive NABH accreditation.
The initiative began on September 25 and will continue until October 15.
People will have the opportunity to learn about their heart health through a cardiac screening package.
Specialist medical consultations will also be available when required.

item.title: Walton, MUN Alert launch initiative to help find missing people
item.description:
Walton Plaza, the country’s largest electronics product sales and service network, has stepped forward with a new initiative to help locate missing people more quickly.
In this regard, Walton Plaza, in collaboration with missing-person alert platform MUN Alert, has launched the ‘Missing Persons Broadcast’ initiative.
Under the initiative, photos and essential information of verified missing persons will be regularly displayed on TV screens at more than 700 Walton Plaza outlets across the country.
In this regard, a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was signed between Walton Plaza and MUN Alert at Walton Corporate Office in the capital on Monday (September 28, 2026).
Mohammad Rayhan, managing director of Walton Plaza, and Sadat Rahman, president of Zero Missing Foundation, the founding organization of MUN Alert, signed the MoU on behalf of their respective organizations.
Among others, Zoheb Ahmed, chief marketing officer of Walton; Masud Parvez, chief executive officer of creative partner Pop5, and officials from the organizations concerned were present at the signing ceremony.
Speaking at the event, Walton Plaza’s Managing Director Mohammad Rayhan said, “Walton Plaza has not confined its activities to product sales and services; rather, it actively participates in various social and humanitarian initiatives for the welfare of the people.
As part of that commitment, we have joined hands with MUN Alert to help disseminate information about missing persons quickly and extensively among the public.”
He said that under the initiative, people will be able to visit their nearest Walton Plaza to view the latest information on missing persons.
When necessary, they will also be able to report a missing person or follow up on an existing report through MUN Alert’s helpline 13219 and its web portal.
Walton’s CMO Zoheb Ahmed said: “A large number of people visit Walton Plaza outlets across the country every day. Using this extensive network and the TV screens at our official outlets to disseminate information about missing persons is part of our social responsibility. We believe this initiative will play an effective role in helping locate missing people quickly and supporting their families.”
MUN Alert founder Sadat Rahman said: “The wider the reach of verified information, the greater the possibility of finding a missing person. Walton Plaza’s extensive nationwide network will help take missing-person information to many places that would otherwise be difficult for us to reach on our own. We are delighted to have Walton Plaza by our side in this humanitarian initiative.”

item.title: President urges research, innovation in emerging technologies
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir has called for greater research and innovation in modern digital technology, artificial intelligence (AI), nanotechnology, biotechnology and semiconductors for public welfare.
He also stressed the need for responsible and measured use of AI.
The President made the remarks on Tuesday when a delegation from Khulna University of Engineering & Technology (KUET), led by Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Muhammad Masud, paid a courtesy call on him at Bangabhaban.
He cautioned against the uncontrolled and indiscriminate use of AI, saying excessive reliance on the technology could undermine people’s thinking abilities and creativity. He stressed ensuring its measured use for public welfare.
During the meeting, the KUET vice-chancellor briefed the President on the university’s overall academic activities.
The President stressed the need to decentralise quality education beyond the capital and increase universities’ involvement in national research and development activities.
The vice-chancellor also formally invited the President to attend KUET’s upcoming convocation as chancellor. The President accepted the invitation and assured the delegation of his attendance.
The President’s military secretary, secretary and press secretary, along with KUET professors, were present at the meeting.

item.title: Health minister: No warning signs of heart disease should be ignored
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain on Tuesday urged people not to ignore any warning signs or symptoms of heart disease, stressing that public awareness is crucial to preventing and controlling cardiovascular diseases.
“Most people die from heart disease among non-communicable diseases. So, there is no alternative to raising awareness for preventing and controlling heart disease,” he said while addressing a discussion as the chief guest at the Hotel InterContinental in the capital.
The Bangladesh Cardiac Society organized the discussion with its Convener Professor Dr Mohammad Shafiuddin in the chair to mark the World Heart Day 2026, said a press release.
Sakhawat said people are aware of the importance of health awareness, but often fail to put that awareness into practice in their daily lives.
“This tendency is particularly risky in the case of heart disease,” he said, urging people to seek medical advice promptly instead of ignoring any warning signs or symptoms related to the heart.
The minister said public awareness is equally important for the prevention and control of all types of diseases, both communicable and non-communicable.
Describing physicians as the noblest members of society, Sakhawat said after the Creator, doctors are the trusted source of support for people in times of distress.
“From the coronavirus pandemic to dengue and various natural disasters, doctors and health workers have remained engaged in serving people without thinking about their own lives and safety,” he said, adding that their humanitarian and professional commitment is exemplary for the people of the country.
Director General of the Directorate General of Medical Education Professor Dr Nazmul Hosain and Assistant Personal Physician to the Prime Minister Dr ANM Monowarul Kadir attended the program, among others, as special guests.
Dr AF Khabiruddin Ahmed supervised the overall arrangements.
Earlier, the minister formally inaugurated World Heart Day by releasing balloons at the premises of the BMU Super Specialized Hospital and participated in a rally organised marking the day.

item.title: Md Mejba Uddin Ali appointed new chairman of BUFT Board of Trustees
item.description:
Md Mejba Uddin Ali, chairman of Wega Group, has been appointed chairman of the newly constituted Board of Trustees (BoT) of BGMEA University of Fashion & Technology (BUFT).
The appointment was made at the board’s inaugural meeting on Monday, where members discussed key issues related to the university’s governance, administration and future development.
The newly constituted board reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening BUFT’s academic and institutional capabilities and supporting its continued growth and development.
The meeting also highlighted the importance of enhancing the university’s contribution to education and professional skills development in Bangladesh’s textile, apparel and fashion industries.
Against this backdrop, the board discussed strategic initiatives to further align BUFT’s academic programs and skills development efforts with the evolving needs of the industry.

item.title: Infantino ready to increase funding for all 211 members
item.description:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino has opened the door to substantial increases in funding for the world governing body's 211 members, with the FIFA Council set to consider additional payments at its meeting on October 15.
In a letter sent to the presidents of FIFA's six continental confederations on Monday, and seen by Agence Frannce-Presse, Infantino said he would support "the greatest level of additional funding that can responsibly be delivered", but cautioned that no figure currently under discussion represented an approved commitment.
Infantino said the abandoned proposal to sell a slice of the World Cup commercial rights that brought calls for his resignation had been intended to generate additional money for football.
"The recent commercial proposal, now withdrawn, was intended to enable FIFA to invest more in football," Infantino wrote.
On September 18, two of Infantino's critics, European football chief Aleksander Ceferin and his counterpart at the North and Central American and Caribbean body, Victor Montagliani, said each of FIFA's member associations ) should receive $10 million in the four years between 2027-2030.
Infantino responded by suggesting he would match any other offers.
"I will support the greatest level of additional funding that can responsibly be delivered through FIFA's proper governance process," he said.
FIFA confirmed in early September that Infantino will stand for president in an election next March, despite the backlash over his now-abandoned plan to bring private investment into the men's and women's World Cups.
Infantino is not without friends -- 2034 World Cup hosts Saudi Arabia came out in support last month, with African football's governing body CAF and South America's CONMEBOL also supportive.

item.title: Manchester City's Premier League charges: What comes next?
item.description:
Manchester City's fate in a legal battle with the Premier League is yet to be sealed, but reports they have been found guilty on widespread financial misconduct has sparked speculation of what comes next.
The dominant Premier League force for more than a decade, swingeing sanctions against City would send shockwaves through English football.
Rival clubs are set to launch their own legal action seeking hundreds of millions of pounds in compensation, while there is debate over whether some of City's many titles and trophies over the past 15 years could be stripped.
AFP Sports looks at the next steps and potential fall out from the case:
Sanction and appeals process
The Athletic first reported on Friday that City had been found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges they faced.
However, no sanction has yet been approved.
Even once a decision is made on how City will be punished, should they be found guilty, the club are almost certain to appeal.
In a letter to City fans on Saturday, the club's chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said: "Our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began."
A case that began after German outlet Der Spiegel published leaked documents from City executives in 2018, could still take a lengthy time to fully resolve.
According to Premier League rules, the sanction can vary from a points deduction, a fine or even expulsion from the division.
Everton and Nottingham Forest were handed points deductions in the 2023/24 season for single breaches of financial sustainability rules. On that basis, City would face almost certain relegation if found guilty of over 100 charges.
Whether the sanction is applied before an appeal is heard will be another bone of contention.
If it is, City could face relegation before overturning any guilty verdict.
On the other hand, if City, who currently sit top of the table, are not punished until after an appeal, it could cost other clubs their place in the top-flight or lucrative European qualification.
Even after the Premier League process if over, there is also the chance that City's Abu-Dhabi backed owners seek redress in England's High Court if they challenge a legal issue regarding how the arbitration process was conducted.
Who stands to gain?
City's rivals were quick to revel in the news of their potential demise.
"Another Premier League medal to be added to the cabinet," posted former Manchester United defender Rio Ferdinand, who was part of the United team to finish second to City in the 2011/12 season.
The reality is that stripping and retroactively awarding titles is a messy process.
City's charges relate to the period between 2009 and 2018. In that time they won four league titles, with United and Liverpool twice finishing second in those seasons.
Yet City have won another four since, arguably built on foundations that were fraudulently gained.
They also won four League Cups and one FA Cup, the club's first trophy for 35 years, in the period between 2009 and 2018.
"I don't seriously believe any other trophies and titles will be handed back over either," Tony Pulis, whose Stoke side lost the 2011 FA Cup final to City, told the BBC.
"A points deduction and a massive fine feels far more likely. But I still feel cheated."
A more likely source of recompense for clubs that missed out is through financial compensation.
In June, Everton were told they must pay Burnley œ35 million ($46 million) after they edged out the Clarets to Premier League survival in the same season they broke financial sustainability rules.
What about City's stars?
Less than a month ago, City completed the biggest ever transfer spend in one window, splashing out around œ460 million on the likes of Enzo Fernandez, Elliott Anderson and Ayyoub Bouaddi.
The impending verdict on the charges has to this point made little impact on City's ability to attract and retain their star names.
Talismanic striker Erling Haaland signed a nine-year contract in 2025 that could keep him tied down till his 34th birthday.
How many, if any, of the players managed to negotiate exit clauses in the case City were heavily sanctioned remains to be seen.

item.title: Ruthless An makes history to retain Asian Games badminton crown
item.description:
South Korea's badminton world number one An Se-young became the first woman to win two Asian Games singles titles after dominating Japan's Akane Yamaguchi 21-17, 21-9 in Tuesday's final.
The reigning Olympic and world champion, who has not lost a match since March, gave another ruthless display in Nagoya to defend the Asian Games title she won three years ago in Hangzhou.
It was the 24-year-old's eighth title of an incredible 2026.
Of those she didn't win, she finished runner-up at the All-England Open and pulled out injured from the Japan Open.
She won her second world title in August in New Delhi.
Backed by pockets of vocal Korean fans in the arena, An made a slow start but battled back and took control of the first game.
She sent Yamaguchi sprawling with one smash to the line, before clinching the first game with a backhand flick at the net.
An kept up her assault in the second game, building a big lead to make her latest title look inevitable.
It arrived when Yamaguchi hit a serve return long, and An celebrated by dropping to her knees and letting out a primal scream.
An had already beaten Yamaguchi this week in the women's team event.
The world number one has been in feisty form at the Asian Games, apologising after her frustration threatened to boil over in an earlier match.
She also had stern words for her watching father, saying: "I am out there running myself into the ground and he is just cheering away in comfort."
Fellow South Koreans Lee So-hee and Baek Ha-na won the women's double gold after a marathon 26-28, 21-18, 21-18 win over China's Liu Shengshu and Tan Ning.
The match was poised at 18-each in the final game when Liu went down with an ankle injury.
She managed to continue but the Korean pair took advantage to close out the match.
China's Jiang Zhenbang and Wei Yaxin won the mixed doubles final, beating Indonesia's Amri Syahnawi and Nita Violina Marwah 21-19, 21-8.

item.title: Tobacco control must not be ignored
item.description:
We absolutely agree that while Bangladesh has taken an important step by amending its tobacco control law, the immediate priority must now be to formulate the rules needed to make the amended law effective.
Experts have rightly called for the rules to be prepared without delay. The amended law was passed in April, strengthening several areas of tobacco control, but its provisions will have limited impact if there is uncertainty over how they are to be enforced.
This is particularly urgent given the scale of tobacco use in Bangladesh. According to figures cited at a recent discussion, 35.3% of the population uses tobacco, while tobacco-related deaths and economic losses impose a substantial burden on the country.
Research from the Institute of Health Economics estimated tobacco-generated government revenue at around Tk41,000 crore in FY25, against an annual economic cost of approximately Tk87,000 crore.
These figures should make clear that tobacco control is not simply a matter of individual choice. It is a public health, economic, and regulatory issue that affects families, healthcare systems, and productivity.
The rules must therefore be comprehensive and enforceable, and address gaps involving emerging nicotine products, single-stick cigarette sales, and the regulation of smoking areas, while ensuring that tobacco companies cannot exploit ambiguities in the law.
Experts have also stressed the importance of aligning implementation with Bangladesh's commitments under the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control.
Most importantly, there must be no prolonged gap between passing a law and putting its supporting rules in place.
Bangladesh has already established the legal foundation. The next responsibility lies with the relevant authorities to ensure that the rules are formulated carefully, transparently, and swiftly, followed by consistent enforcement.
Public health cannot remain dependent on legislation that exists on paper. The real measure of this reform will be whether it produces a meaningful reduction in tobacco exposure and its consequences

item.title: Beyond the bottom line
item.description:
The Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) opened its January spectrum auction, expecting the high-stakes competition typical of vital national infrastructure sales. Instead, the room fell silent.
Grameenphone acquired 10 MHz of the 700 MHz band at the base reserve price of Tk2,370 crore, Robi withdrew, while Banglalink stayed away from the bidding, leaving 10 MHz of the unsold spectrum to be assigned later to state-owned Teletalk at the same rate.
Failing to attract competition, this transaction left policy-makers with a critical question: How can such an auction dictate the pricing of an upcoming renewal cycle?
The short answer is it cannot . True market value requires viable alternatives where operators bid for expansion, not survival. Spectrum renewal offers no such luxury.
Once a mobile operator anchors its network architecture around a specific band and deploys thousands of base stations, walking away is no longer an option. A renewal price has little to do with market value; it is apparently a reflection of short-term state treasury demands colliding with an operator's inability to walk away without shutting down their business.
This structural disconnect matters as Bangladesh approaches the November renewal of spectrum in the 900 MHz, 1.8 GHz, and 2.1 GHz bands. Data from the GSMA’s 2025 study reveals that Bangladesh’s spectrum costs consume 15.7% of operators’ recurring revenues, much higher than the Asia-Pacific median of 10.4% and the global median of 7.7%.
Macroeconomic modeling suggests that cutting this economic burden to half could unlock $34 billion in cumulative economic benefits by 2035 and a 75% reduction could generate $45bn. These numbers are no prescription to slash prices; rather, they must be weighed against the state’s undeniable fiscal duty to manage a public asset.
At the same time, operators need capital for advanced radios and network upgrades. The real policy challenge is not finding an arbitrary, magic price per megahertz, but ensuring that every megahertz becomes highly productive.
Spectrum productivity is best measured by its capacity for dense urban hubs, wider coverage for rural villages, and reliable network quality during peak hours. Yet, BTRC data exposes a deep structural imbalance in our airwaves.
State-owned Teletalk holds 65.2 MHz for just 6.8 million subscribers, while Grameenphone must squeeze 84.4 million subscribers into 137.4 MHz. Serving remote terrain explains part of this gap, but not all of it.
When rigid frameworks lock spectrum in underutilized silos while urban networks suffer from congestion, the scarcity becomes artificial. Because traffic patterns shift constantly, a band that was adequate five years ago may leave one city congested today while sitting idle in another. If frequency blocks cannot move dynamically to match this shifting public demand, the consumer experience inevitably degrades, and the broader digital economy suffers.
Other nations have long recognized that draining an operator's capital through high upfront spectrum fees may starve the investments needed for network rollouts. Many have shifted toward models that trade immediate financial burdens for guaranteed socio-economic outcomes.
India addressed artificial scarcity by legalizing spectrum trading and sharing , allowing rights to move toward operators facing heavy traffic. Its framework permitted transfers subject to spectrum caps, roll-out obligations, eligibility conditions and a two-year holding period, with a 1% transfer fee.
Similarly, Austria and Colombia tied their low-band spectrum licensing directly to rural coverage, allowing operators to earn explicit fee discounts or convert coverage commitments into cash-equivalent credits. Spain and Canada chose to extend license terms or waive upfront renewal fees where operators could demonstrate minimum population coverage , giving companies the necessary breathing room to amortize massive hardware investments.
The warnings from the global markets should also be watched closely. In its multi-band auction, Pakistan cut reserve prices on legacy bands by more than 50%, yet those bands still drew no bids.
This proved that artificial benchmarks fail to create demand for spectrum that lacks commercial viability. In contrast, Vietnam demonstrates the power of flexible strategic asset pricing; after a failed 2023 auction, it slashed reserve prices by nearly 80%, separating long-term economic utility from the temptation of short-term cash extraction to rapidly achieve roughly 90% 5G coverage by early 2026.
Meanwhile, other regulatory experiments show distinct operational challenges: Austria faced ambiguity over how coverage would be measured. Colombia’s process was criticized for hiding minimum bids in advance while miscalculating rural rollout costs.
Finally, Canada’s model serves as a direct warning; its rigid obligation conditions drove up holding costs without incentivizing efficient use, creating long-term operational inefficiencies after the regulator ignored industry challenges during consultations.
To break out of the cycle of revenue-maximizing deadlocks and deteriorating network quality, Bangladesh needs a pragmatic, forward-looking approach. Rather than exhausting operator liquidity through high upfront hurdles, BTRC can incentivize infrastructure development by recalibrating its renewal fees into a more manageable, back-loaded payment timeline.
To protect the state’s interests, the time value of money can be maintained through transparent indexation, while operators preserve the vital cash flow.
Furthermore, the regulator can introduce an infrastructure offset mechanism . Operators should be allowed to discharge a defined portion of their renewal fees through verified capital investments in high-priority public infrastructure.
To ensure transparency, these projects must be selected from a pre-approved national registry, such as expanding coverage in deep rural unions, and undergo rigorous independent valuation.
This framework must carry strict non-delivery penalties and exclude any publicly subsidized projects to prevent double counting.
Crucially, these renewed licenses should mandate measurable outcomes:
Such a spectrum-for-investment bargain remains credible if the measurement framework is indisputable. Methodology, sampling, thresholds, and audit rights must be fixed before renewal.
Bangladesh has learned this the hard way; a Tk 21 crore network quality testing system deployed by the BTRC in 2022 failed to yield a conclusive public report for years simply because the regulator and operators could not agree on measurement metrics.
Fortunately, that gap is finally closing with the commission’s recent approval of a tighter, collaboratively developed drive-test protocol, which provides the necessary baseline for future enforcement.
Frequency blocks must be allowed to flow where the users essentially are. The BTRC should formalize a secondary market framework that permits operators to lease or temporarily transfer underutilized spectrum under clear competition rules.
This must be backed by a strict anti-hoarding policy. If an operator leaves an assigned band materially underused across a specific region for more than 18 months, they must deploy it against agreed performance indicators, open it for voluntary localized sharing, or surrender it back to the national pool.
This flexibility should be driven by real-time monitoring. Instead of allowing expensive auditing tools to sit idle, the regulator should leverage its updated field-testing capabilities to publish monthly, region-specific network performance reports.
Linking continued spectrum retention to these localized, busy-hour quality audits will transform transparency into an enforcement tool, forcing operators to prioritize real-world delivery over asset hoarding.
The current policy standoff is primarily behavioral -- regulators are historically evaluated on immediate treasury targets, while operators pile up spectrum to protect market share without optimizing performance.
We must redefine what institutional achievement looks like in telecommunication governance. A spectrum renewal cycle should not be evaluated by the volume of cash deposited into the treasury on day one.
Instead, its true dividends should be measured by expanded coverage, fewer dropped calls, faster internet speeds, and the seamless rollout of next-generation 5G networks.
On the corporate side, operators must be pushed to move away from vanity metrics. Total SIM card registrations tell us really nothing about actual digital utility.
Instead, the regulatory framework should compel corporations to publicly report active data users per megahertz per base station.
This simple shift forces corporate focus toward capital efficiency and network optimization rather than defensive asset hoarding.
A high spectrum price functions as a regressive tax on the end consumer, directly stalling smartphone adoption and digital literacy in underserved communities.
By lowering upfront spectrum barriers and ensuring sufficient capacity, the per-gigabyte cost for operators drops.
The regulatory framework must ensure these savings are passed down to low-income tiers through affordable, high-volume data packages tailored for students, marginal farmers, and micro-entrepreneurs.
Directing infrastructure offsets specifically toward hard-to-reach and climate-vulnerable coastal communities ensures that our digital safety net, including mobile financial services, telemedicine, and online education, becomes accessible for the whole population, rather than a privilege concentrated within a few major metropolitan centers.
By November, the thousands of telecommunication antennas stretching across Bangladesh’s skylines will point exactly where they point today. The critical question for our future is whether the licenses governing those radio frequencies will simply preserve a congested network or lay the groundwork for tomorrow's digital economy.
A cheap megahertz that remains underutilized does nothing for national development. An overpriced megahertz that depletes an operator's investment capacity behaves no differently.
The state does not hold the radio spectrum to act as a mere fee collector; it holds it in trust as a scarce public resource. The real test of the upcoming renewal cycle is not how much revenue the state collects per megahertz; it is the quality of the digital nation emerging on the ground.
Dr Sabbir Ahmad is a tech executive with global experience in digital connectivity, sustainable infrastructure and energy. He is shaping Bangladesh's semiconductor landscape as the CEO of Silicon Array Ltd. Email: sabbir@ieee.org .

item.title: WHO: Yemen health system at ‘breaking point’
item.description:
The escalating fighting in Yemen is pushing the country’s health system to “breaking point”, the World Health Organization said Tuesday, warning that diseases like cholera were already circulating widely.
A renewed ground campaign waged by the Iran-backed Houthis against Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces has left hundreds dead and is deepening the country’s humanitarian crisis, with at least 145,000 people displaced this month alone, United Nations figures show.
And the country’s health system -- already weakened by over a decade of civil war -- is on the brink.
“Yemen’s latest escalation is pushing an already fragile health system towards breaking point,” warned Annette Heinzelmann, WHO’s emergency director for the eastern Mediterranean region.
Speaking to reporters in Geneva via video link from Cairo, she highlighted how insecurity, damaged infrastructure, displacement of health workers, shortages of medicines and medical supplies and limited access to swathes of Yemen’s west coast were preventing many from receiving the services they need.
“Nine health facilities or assets have now been damaged, put out of service, closed or directly attacked” in the hard-hit areas of Taiz, Lahj and Hodeidah, Heinzelmann said.
At the same time, “comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care has been suspended in two hospitals in Marib and Ras Al-Arah because staff and operating capacity have been redirected to trauma care for the incoming wounded,” she pointed out.
Even before the latest escalation, only around 60 percent of Yemen’s health facilities were fully functional, Heinzelmann added.
And the country had been facing high malnutrition and outbreaks of diseases like cholera “already circulating on a large scale,” she said.
Since the start of this year, Yemen has tallied nearly 8,000 suspected cholera cases, including 22 deaths, and more than 9,600 dengue cases, including 37 people who had died, according to the WHO.
And “measles is particularly concerning, with more than 22,000 suspected cases and 128 deaths reported this year,” Heinzelmann said.
Now, amidst severe overcrowding in some areas, unsanitary conditions and limited healthcare access, the WHO is bracing for more and bigger disease outbreaks.
“When we see population movements, people living in really... an overcrowded setting with limited access to water and safe sanitation, these are factors which can support a wider spread of cholera,” Heinzelmann said.
The UN health agency said it had delivered nearly 60 tons of medical supplies to 40 facilities across 10 Yemen governorates.
“But several lifesaving supply lines in WHO’s Aden warehouse are already at zero stock, including trauma kits and essential medicines,” Heinzelmann said, appealing for more funding.
WHO had so far secured only $2 million of the $9 million it needed for its response, she said.

item.title: OpenAI shelves new AI model amid safety concerns
item.description:
Artificial intelligence company OpenAI has abandoned plans to release a next-generation AI model after internal testing found that the system failed to meet the company’s safety and alignment standards.
GPT-6.1 Astra, which is designed to handle increasingly complex tasks with less human intervention, had been scheduled to debut in October but tests reportedly found that the model displayed higher levels of deceptive behavior than its predecessors.
Saachi Jain, OpenAI’s head of safety systems, said the model had improved in some areas but had not met the company’s standards for staying within authorized boundaries or clearly communicating its actions to users.
“We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that’s in the company, or when we ship it to users,” Jain said. “But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms ⁠of safety and ​alignment.”
The postponement comes as OpenAI and other AI companies face growing pressure to strengthen safeguards around increasingly powerful and autonomous models.
Some of these models developed by OpenAI and rival lab Anthropic have been involved in security incidents during testing.
Earlier this month, OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman and Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei joined other industry leaders in calling for a slower pace of AI development and stronger safety measures.
Leading AI executives are set to meet with US President Donald Trump in Washington on Tuesday to discuss the need for finding a balance between AI innovation and oversight.
On Tuesday, OpenAI admitted that its models had even accessed Australian government websites and systems without authorization as part of internal training and evaluation exercises in June.
The company said ‌the activity ‌involved ​websites and systems linked to Services Australia, ​the NSW Bureau of ⁠Crime ​Statistics and Research, ​the Victorian ​Department of ‌Health and the Australian ​Institute ⁠of Health and ⁠Welfare.
The incursion, which occurred in June, was not made public until last week.
In a blog post, the ChatGPT maker apologized for the hacking and acknowledged it ‌mishandled its response ⁠and ⁠pledged to take accountability to “rebuild trust with the Australian people.”

item.title: Malaysia starts sending Myanmar migrants home
item.description:
Malaysia began sending back around 1,500 Myanmar nationals Tuesday, AFP journalists saw, launching a scheme rights groups say may endanger migrants by returning them to the war-torn country.
The batch is the first of 5,000 Myanmar citizens Kuala Lumpur says agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centers amidst a huge uptick in anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.
But advocacy organizations say dire conditions in detention centers may have forced their decisions, and they could face dangerous homecomings in Myanmar where war has raged since 2021.
Neither Malaysia nor Myanmar have officially clarified the number of Rohingya in the first group, and there is concern they may be returned to a country where they face persecution rights groups say amounts to genocide.
Dozens of buses arrived under police escort on Tuesday at the Majlis Perbandaran Manjung stadium near the Lumut naval base in northwestern Malaysia, AFP correspondents saw, where the migrants were to be processed.
They will then be transported to the nearby naval base and taken to Myanmar by ship.
A Myanmar security source, requesting anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to media, said the boats are due to dock at Thanlyin Navy Base just south of Yangon around the end of this week.
Marine traffic websites showed Myanmar’s auxiliary support and hospital ship Than Lwin at anchor just outside the naval base.
Rohingya, a persecuted Muslim minority, make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the United Nations.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced in July that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 members of the Rohingya.
The plan was announced after authorities detained more than 100 Rohingya who had gathered outside the UN refugee agency’s office in Kuala Lumpur.
They were seeking help after being threatened with eviction from an informal settlement in northern Penang state.
They were later released after officials confirmed they held valid UN documentation.
Myanmar earlier this month pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the United Nations and rights groups.
Last week more than 160 civil society groups in a joint statement called upon the Malaysian government to “immediately halt the deportations,” pending talks with civil organizations about the situation on the ground in Myanmar.
Anwar said he would invite Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-civilian president Min Aung Hlaing for an official visit to help expedite the repatriation process.
But the civil groups urged that “Malaysia’s engagement with the junta must not come at the expense of its own reputation and integrity.”
Malaysia’s home affairs ministry last month said 5,000 individuals will undergo voluntary repatriation as agreed by the Myanmar government.
There were 10,388 Myanmar nationals held at immigration detention depots by mid-August, the ministry said, with not all considered refugees.
Malaysia, which shelters one of Southeast Asia’s biggest refugee populations, is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognize refugee status.
AFP fact-checkers have found that Rohingya refugees in Malaysia have been targeted by online disinformation campaigns that rights advocates say are fueling xenophobia and intimidation.
Many of the Rohingya, a mostly Muslim group, escaped Myanmar during a brutal military crackdown in 2017.
Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled Myanmar after the offensive, which is the basis of a genocide case at the International Court of Justice.
More than 1.2 million live just over the border in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement, but talk of repatriations from there has yielded little progress.

item.title: Iran threatens new strikes as it awaits US response to Hormuz plan
item.description:
Iran on Tuesday threatened to attack infrastructure around the Middle East, intensifying its rhetoric as it awaits a formal response from Washington on a new plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
US President Donald Trump has already dismissed the proposal from Tehran, but Iran’s foreign minister said Monday that he was expecting a formal response from American officials in the coming day.
Fighting has subsided in recent weeks, though Tehran has continued to target ships in the strait, with Washington falling back on an economic pressure campaign instead of further military action.
Iran’s chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Tuesday threatened new attacks, saying no infrastructure in the region would be safe if his country’s security was not guaranteed.
“In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one else will sell oil either; or if our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will remain safe,” Ghalibaf, who is also Iran’s parliament speaker, said according to video released by state TV.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he expected a formal answer from the US on Tuesday to Tehran’s proposal, state media reported.
Iran has maintained a blockade on commercial shipping through Hormuz since the war began in late February with US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic.
The shipping route carried a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas before the conflict began.
The US military has been maintaining a counterblockade of Iran’s ports in an effort to prevent Tehran from exporting oil.
Araghchi said late Monday that Qatari intermediaries “presented ideas, and we discussed them; they are set to raise the matter with the American side once more, after which the final US response will be conveyed to us.”
The top diplomat, who was in New York for the UN General Assembly, said “The Qataris hope this will be done by tomorrow.”
“The current focus is solely on the Strait of Hormuz, and the reopening of the strait is contingent upon the fulfilment of certain conditions that we have communicated to the other side,” he added.
Last week, discussions were held in New York between Araghchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
As a precondition for ending its blockade, Iran is demanding a seven-day ceasefire across the Middle East, including in Lebanon, where its ally Hezbollah is regularly bombarded by Israel.
It is also demanding the unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade on its ports.
Both sides claim to have control of Hormuz, with the US saying oil is moving through and Tehran insisting the waterway is closed.
On Tuesday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of the country’s military, said “the US claim that it remains open is false.”
“Sneaking a few hundred barrels of oil through under the cover of darkness -- with transponders turned off and at great cost -- does not constitute the strait being open,” said spokesperson Hossein Mohebi.
“A truly open strait is one where, as in the past, at least 125 vessels would pass through daily, transporting a minimum of 20 million barrels of oil and petroleum products.
“Any vessel attempting to pass through sustains damage -- either we strike it, or it hits a mine,” he added.

item.title: Building bridges: Lessons from Ta-Nehisi Coates
item.description:
“There is more wisdom in your body than in your deepest philosophy.”
Between the World & Me (Spiegel & Grau, 2015) by Ta-Nehisi Coates is a book-length exposition of racism in the United States.
True to the advice from Nietzsche above, he explores the topic not through philosophical musings but through the brutal lived experience.
Written as a letter to his son, Samori, the book is an archive of Coates’ personal life through the Black neighborhood.
Although Coates’ book is centered around his experiences growing up as a Black person in the United States, his words reflect every colonized nationality in history.
And what gets lost in the cold, dry words of history, sociology, and statistics is how much the legacy of racism still lingers on to this day.
Coates analyses how Black bodies are not their own but are still very much at the hand of their colonizers, despite how much the colonizers want to think otherwise.
He wants us to dig deeper into who the "people" are in Lincoln’s “Democracy is government by, for and of the people”?
Questioning the US’ claim of being the greatest nation on earth, Coates is skeptical whether the police who murder Black teenagers in the streets in broad daylight disproportionately truly go against the ideals of their nation. Or are they the proud progeny of the country’s history?
The US, or for that matter almost every empire on the face of the earth, has been built on blood.
Today, Israel continues to do the same with Palestinians; the only difference is this time the world has the internet to see everything. Every colonizer has a history of genocide.
That’s evident in Coates’ book when he describes his visit to Paris. He understands that being Black there is not the same as in the US, but that supposedly noble country is also built on the backs of Algerians.
All of this is to elicit the simple question: can racism be solved if only people are good at their intentions? Coates thinks the answer is "NO."
History has been unfair to the oppressed, and the unfairness continues its legacy. Black neighborhoods don’t have better schools because of being located in suburbs, which is a direct result of segregationist policies of a not-so-distant time.
The colonizers have to recognize this fact and admit that the problem is not only because of individual acts but also the history, policies and economics that remain hidden.
Admitting this can result in a broken dream, as Coates refers to continuously in his book. Most Americans and the colonizers try their hardest to avoid the question of systemic change, focusing only on “goodwill” and “good intentions."
They quote Martin Luther King Jr.’s famous speech “I Have a Dream," where he wants his children to be judged by their character, not by their skin, pointing to that as the goal.
But they conveniently leave out the fact that he also advocated systemic changes and reparations his whole life, and was hated by the racists all over the country in his time.
The US is terrified of its history. From whitewashing the narrative of Thanksgiving to anti-CRT mania, this fact has been vindicated. Similar stories have been told to justify the oppression of the natives here as well: the British were the civilizers of the savages here.
But, as promised, Coates forces us to focus on the daily effects of racism. He recalls the fear he saw in his elders, who got terrified when a child got lost while playing in the park.
He remembers his father saying, “Either I beat him or the police," which was a method of control so that children would be cautious of the world around them and not get killed.
He doesn’t want his son, Samori, to be “tough” or acquainted with the street attitude but can’t shake off the fear that one day he will lose him too, just as he lost his friend at Howard University due to police violence.
He talks about his wife and other Black women and realizes that, as whites couldn’t always bridge the gap between their world and his, similarly he couldn’t always bridge the gap between her world and his. And the bridges can only be traversed through communication and honest inquiry.
But that step is still far away for most Americans. Most of them are happy to include Black and Native people as tokens for diversity, without solving the root issue.
The recent George Floyd case can be an example. After the “Black Lives Matter” protests, many words such as police reform and diversity training were floating around.
Many corporations took a stand with this movement. But as usual, in the end, it was virtue signaling at the corporate and national level.
Keeping one or two Black mayors or a president cannot solve the historical legacy of racism. It has to take into account the legal frameworks that have disadvantaged Black people and the economic issues that have strangled them for decades.
Coates’ book is also significant to understanding how racism can be expressed subtly, which should be a lesson for everyone to be cautious while framing language.
Black History Month is a celebration of all oppressed races on the earth, every native culture that has been destroyed or lost because of imperial ambitions.
Coates searched his whole life to find a way to bridge the gap between his two worlds, how it should be and how it was.
He wants the bridge to vanish for his son so that he can live a true life on his own, in his true body, true self, in a truly free country, not a country free for one race of people.
Black History Month should be directed towards that goal so that every race and ethnicity can bridge the gap between them and their world.
Sadman Ahmed Siam is a student at the Islamic University of Technology.

item.title: Gold Over Rot
item.description:
Sometimes I want so much from God my faith stands in the doorway and refuses to let me ask. I do not ask for houses, for gold, for kingdoms, I ask for gold foil over my sins, something bright enough to hide what is rotten underneath. I ask for pride in who I am, pride in who I shall be tomorrow morning, and still I wake hungry, gluttonous with that disgusting little prayer of more, more, more, until even my hands forget what they were reaching for. Then I am angry with God for giving me nothing. Nothing, when I brought Him my hunger and called it faith, brought Him my weakness and called it fate, brought Him a heart full of wanting and wondered why it never learned how to be full.
Nubisha Rabya Topote, an XI-grade student at Holy Cross College, is a poet and writer who finds inspiration in the world around her. Find more of her work at @nubishawrites.

item.title: Adabor house takeover attempt foiled; 10 arrested
item.description:
Ten people have been arrested in a case filed over an alleged attempt to seize a house, vandalise property and extort money in Adabor, Dhaka, police said.
Four of the suspects, including two who were injured in police gunfire, were arrested during an overnight operation. Police said they opened fire in self-defence after the suspects allegedly attempted to attack officers with machetes.
The incident took place around 2:30am on Monday in an open area beside a canal behind a playground near Kacha Bazar in Naboday Housing, Adabor.
The two injured suspects were identified as Rajib Howlader, 30, and Sagar, 24. Both sustained gunshot wounds to their legs and were taken to Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital for treatment.
The other two arrested during the operation were identified as Shakib, 23, and Rashed, 24.
Adabor police said they launched the operation around 2am based on information about the suspects’ whereabouts. Seven to eight people were present at the scene.
When police attempted to arrest them, the suspects allegedly tried to attack officers with machetes. Police then fired two rounds from a shotgun carried by a constable in self-defence, according to police.
Rajib and Sagar were injured, while the others fled. Police recovered numerous weapons from the scene.
Adabor police station Officer-in-Charge Zahidul Islam said police opened fire after the suspects allegedly attempted to attack them.
“The injured were sent to hospital. Legal action will be taken in connection with the incident,” he said.
The OC said six people had previously been arrested in the case, and the four arrests during the overnight operation brought the total number of suspects arrested to 10.
According to police, Sagar has eight cases filed against him with Adabor and Mohammadpur police stations. Rajib is a named accused in the Babu murder case in Mohammadpur.
Shakib and Rashed each have five cases against them, police said.
On Sunday, a group of 15-20 people allegedly attacked a house in Shyamoli Housing, Adabor, carrying machetes, ramdas and pistols, in an alleged attempt to seize the property.
A case was filed with Adabor police station over the incident.
Police said the two sides had been involved in a longstanding dispute over ownership of the house and that a court case concerning the property is ongoing.

item.title: Social media reshapes childhood, but safety concerns persist
item.description:
The killing of 13-year-old Ishayat Shahriar Apratim in Comilla, who was allegedly lured from his home on the pretext of making a TikTok video, has renewed concerns over the safety of children and teenagers using social media.
Police are investigating several aspects of the case, including Apratim’s contact with older youths, an iPhone, a Tk5,000 debt and the claim that he was called out to make a TikTok video. However, investigators have yet to establish a definitive motive.
Concerns over the risks of social media use among minors are not new. In July, a 20-year-old man was arrested in Feni for allegedly recording and sharing on TikTok an incident involving the harassment of a six-year-old child. In September, a teenage girl was allegedly raped in Comilla after travelling there to meet a young man she had met through Facebook and TikTok.
These incidents cannot simply be attributed to social media. However, they illustrate how children’s and teenagers’ online interactions can have consequences for their safety in the real world.
Several countries have introduced or are considering age restrictions on social media. Australia, Indonesia and Malaysia have adopted different measures for users under 16, while the UK and others are considering similar steps.
In Australia, restrictions on people under 16 opening or maintaining accounts on specified platforms took effect on December 10, 2025. Platforms including Facebook, Instagram, Reddit, Snapchat, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube are required to take “reasonable steps” to prevent under-16s from holding accounts. Children and their parents are not subject to penalties, with primary responsibility placed on the platforms.
Indonesia introduced similar restrictions in March 2026, while Malaysia introduced age-verification requirements on June 1, 2026.
Bangladesh does not currently have a specific minimum age of 16 for opening social media accounts. However, the 2026 Bangladesh Telecommunication (Amendment) Act includes provisions for technical parental controls and, where necessary, age-based verification to protect children and minors using the internet and digital devices and to prevent harassment. Detailed procedures are to be set out in regulations.
Professor Dr M Rezaul Islam of the Institute of Social Welfare and Research at the University of Dhaka said an age limit alone could not eliminate online risks.
“However, restricting children from having personal social media accounts below a certain age may protect them from some online risks. At the same time, social media platforms must be held accountable, while parents should also be given the skills and knowledge needed to ensure digital safety and awareness,” he said.
A 2025 UNICEF Bangladesh U-Report survey, which received responses from around 29,000 children and young people, found that two-thirds identified excessive fake news and misinformation on social media as the biggest source of mental stress. About one in seven cited bullying and negative comments, while a similar proportion identified harmful or upsetting content as a major concern.
The survey also found that 52% of respondents considered rules against harmful behaviour such as bullying and hate speech important, while 79% believed that relaxing such rules could put vulnerable groups at greater risk.
Bangladesh’s expanding internet access means children are increasingly growing up in connected households. The 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics and UNICEF found that 72.1% of households have internet access at home.
The BBS ICT Access and Use by Households and Individuals Survey 2024–25 found that 53.4% of people in Bangladesh use the internet, including 75.7% in urban areas and 43.6% in rural areas. However, the survey does not specifically measure internet use among children.
A 2025 study published in BMJ Open , involving 456 students aged 13–18 at four schools in urban and rural Bangladesh, found that about 88% used the internet. Mobile phones were the primary means of access for 84% of respondents. The study was not nationally representative.
Globally, internet use among young people is also widespread. According to 2025 data from the International Telecommunication Union, 82% of people aged 15–24 use the internet, compared with 72% among those outside that age group.
The World Health Organization’s Health Behaviour in School-aged Children study, which analysed data from around 280,000 adolescents aged 11, 13 and 15 across 44 countries and regions, found that problematic social media use rose from 7% in 2018 to 11% in 2022. The rate was 13% among girls and 9% among boys.
Psychiatrist Dr Bulbul Ahmed Khan said adolescents may not always be able to assess the long-term consequences of communicating with strangers online, taking part in risky challenges or being exposed to harmful content in the same way as adults because parts of the brain involved in risk assessment, emotional control and decision-making are still developing.
“Therefore, children need age-appropriate protection and guidance from adults in their online experiences up to a certain age. However, simply imposing restrictions or setting an age limit will not solve the problem. Open communication within the family, digital literacy, the ability to identify online risks and mental health support when necessary all need to be ensured together,” he said.
Belayet Hossain, a resident of Azimpur, said his Class 8 child uses a phone for studies and communication, but he worries about what the child does online and who they communicate with.
“Simply taking the phone away will not solve the problem,” he said, adding that he tries to maintain open communication so his child feels comfortable telling the family if a stranger makes contact or a problem arises online.
“Social media platforms should also take children’s safety more seriously,” he added.
Another key question is how an age limit would be implemented.
Professor Dr M Rezaul Islam said requiring children to submit national identity cards, birth registration documents or other personal information to every platform could create new privacy risks.
“Therefore, alongside an age limit, Bangladesh also needs to ensure data minimisation, privacy protection and independent oversight,” he said.
Privacy has also been a key consideration in Australia, where the eSafety Commissioner says age-verification methods must comply with privacy safeguards and users are not required to provide government-issued identification.
Emerging regulatory models also place responsibility on social media platforms, rather than solely on children and their parents. This raises questions over how much responsibility platforms should bear for verifying users’ ages, filtering harmful content, preventing online grooming and protecting children’s accounts.
The government has also acknowledged concerns over harmful content on social media and the need for greater oversight.
Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology Minister Faqir Mahbub Anam said in August that the government was working with social media companies and other stakeholders to regulate harmful content and protect young people from digital risks.
“The ICT Ministry is collaborating with social media companies and relevant stakeholders to establish proper oversight and safeguard our future generation,” he said.
Earlier in July, he told Parliament that the government was working to strengthen coordination with international technology platforms, including YouTube and TikTok, to remove harmful content. He said the government was considering amendments to the Cyber Security Act to improve the process.
China Akter, administrative officer of the Organisation-3 Branch at the Information and Communication Technology Division, said the government was working on measures to ensure a safe digital environment for children, including age-appropriate protection, parental controls and age verification.
“Setting a specific age limit alone cannot reduce online risks. Effective age-verification measures, control of harmful content and responsible practices by social media platforms are also needed,” she said.
“Children should also be made more aware of digital safety, while social media platforms should play a responsible role in creating a safer online environment for them,” she added.
Imtiaz Bin Hafiz, an executive member of Ain o Salish Kendra, said simply telling children not to use certain apps would not protect them from online risks.
“Digital platforms also benefit commercially from children’s participation and engagement. Therefore, responsibility for children’s safety should not rest solely on children and their families. Platforms must also take responsibility and ensure safety measures and child safety by design,” he said.
At the same time, social media can provide children and teenagers with opportunities for education, communication, access to information, creativity and social participation. UNICEF has also noted that digital technology can help children learn, play and communicate, while stressing the need for skills to navigate the digital world safely.
The investigation into Apratim’s killing has once again highlighted how social media can be used to contact and influence children and teenagers. However, the circumstances and motive behind his killing remain under investigation.

item.title: The curious case of 600 ‘lost’ passports a day
item.description:
Nearly 600 Bangladeshi passports are reported lost every day. But many of them may not be “lost” in the conventional sense.
Behind the extraordinary number are passports allegedly withheld by recruiting or visa agencies, documents migrant workers cannot retrieve from employers or intermediaries abroad, and cases in which passports are reported lost, or even deliberately destroyed, in connection with irregular migration, according to findings by the Department of Immigration and Passports.
The scale is striking.
Department sources say 107,300 applications citing lost passports were received in a six-month period, averaging around 17,885 a month and nearly 600 every day.
The volume has become a matter of concern for passport authorities, who are having to process the replacement applications alongside regular applications for new passports and renewals.
It has also prompted the government to tighten the rules for replacing lost, stolen or damaged passports.
While there will be no additional penalty for the first occurrence, anyone reporting a passport lost, stolen or damaged for a second or subsequent time will have to pay an additional Tk10,000 on top of the regular passport fee.
The provision came into effect on September 21 under a new government circular.
But officials say the more intriguing question is what lies behind such a large number of passports being reported lost.
Officials at the Department of Immigration and Passports acknowledge that passports are inevitably lost, stolen or accidentally damaged.
But the scale and circumstances of the applications prompted the department to examine why so many people were seeking replacements.
Officials say they identified three recurring patterns.
The first begins before a traveller even leaves Bangladesh.
Many aspiring migrant workers and travellers hand over their passports to recruiting, travel or visa agencies to process visas.
In some cases, the agencies fail to secure the promised visa but continue to hold the client’s passport while delaying the process with repeated assurances.
Unable to recover the document and desperate to move on, some passport holders eventually file a General Diary with police saying the passport has been lost and use the GD to seek a replacement, officials said.
In effect, the passport may still physically exist, but its holder no longer has access to it.
The second pattern occurs overseas.
Bangladeshi migrant workers sometimes surrender passports to employers, sponsors or agencies while residence and work permits, including iqama in some Middle Eastern countries, are processed.
Problems arise when a worker receives a better job offer or decides to change employment but cannot retrieve the passport.
According to passport officials, some then approach the relevant Bangladesh mission and report the passport lost because they see no other way to obtain a new travel document.
The government’s new rules specifically recognise situations in which a visa agency, individual or institution unlawfully withholds a passport and the holder is unable to recover it.
In such cases, the previous passport can be revoked and a replacement issued through the prescribed procedure.
The third category identified by officials is more sensitive.
Passport authorities say some cases are connected to irregular migration.
According to officials, people who enter or remain in another country through irregular channels may seek a new passport after reporting the original lost.
In some cases, they said, a passport may even be deliberately destroyed or discarded before its holder seeks another one.
The department has not provided a breakdown of the 107,300 applications showing how many fall into each of these categories.
The explanations therefore represent patterns identified by passport officials and should not be taken to mean that most or all lost-passport applications involve deliberate misrepresentation.
Nevertheless, officials say the findings help explain why the number of replacement applications has reached a level that can no longer be treated simply as a matter of people accidentally misplacing documents.
As applications continued to pile up, the Department of Immigration and Passports raised the issue with the Home Ministry during the previous interim government’s tenure.
Several meetings were subsequently held to consider how repeated passport losses could be discouraged.
Officials said policymakers were conscious that a Tk10,000 penalty would be substantial for many Bangladeshis given prevailing socio-economic conditions.
Ultimately, however, they decided against penalising someone for a first incident while imposing a significantly higher cost on repeated cases.
Under the new system, a person reporting a passport lost, stolen or damaged for the first time will pay only the regular fee required for reissuance.
From the second occurrence onwards, the applicant will have to pay an additional Tk10,000 each time.
The new rules were formalised through a government circular issued on September 21 and signed by Deputy Secretary Mohammad Nuruzzaman.
The circular also lays down a more structured procedure for dealing with lost, stolen and damaged passports.
A passport holder must immediately report the incident through the designated online system of the Department of Immigration and Passports and simultaneously file a General Diary at the nearest police station.
Police will then have 72 hours to verify the GD and submit a report.
If no police verification report is received within that period, the applicant can proceed with the reissuance process by submitting a copy of the GD, after which a “Lost Circular” will be initiated.
The procedure is intended not only to facilitate replacement but also to ensure that a passport reported missing is quickly identified within immigration and law-enforcement systems.
Information on a lost or stolen passport will be entered into the Special Branch’s Immigration Management System immediately after the report is received.
INTERPOL may also be informed where necessary.
The circular separately addresses one of the problems identified during the department’s investigation, passports being withheld by third parties.
If a visa agency, individual or institution unlawfully keeps someone’s passport and efforts to retrieve it fail, the holder can seek revocation of the original document and issuance of a new passport.
This means passport holders in such circumstances will have a formal route to seek replacement rather than continuing indefinitely without access to their travel document.
Bangladeshis who lose their passports overseas must report the matter to the relevant Bangladesh embassy, high commission or other diplomatic mission.
The mission will issue the necessary Lost Circular and process the application for reissuance.
Replacement will not completely erase the history of the missing document.
The data page of a passport reissued following a reported loss will state: “Previous Passport is Reported to be Lost.”
Applicants will also not be able to use the reissuance process to change fundamental identity information such as their name, parents’ names or date of birth.
That provision is intended to ensure continuity between the identity attached to the cancelled passport and the replacement document.
The new rules also address what happens when someone finds a passport after already reporting it lost.
Once the original passport has been revoked, recovering it does not make it valid again.
The holder cannot use the recovered passport for international travel and must notify the relevant authorities or police so that the document can be dealt with according to procedure.
The restriction is significant because a passport reported lost or stolen may already have been entered into immigration databases as an invalid travel document.
ATM Abu Asad, additional director general for passport, visa and immigration at the Department of Immigration and Passports, said the volume of applications involving lost, stolen or damaged passports had become a concern.
“We have issued certain guidelines to raise awareness among passport holders,” he told Bangla Tribune.
“We have not imposed any additional fee for the first instance,” he said.
“However, an extra Tk10,000 has been set as a penalty for a second occurrence. This measure is intended solely to foster awareness.”
The department’s message, he said, was ultimately about responsibility.
“Our appeal is for passport holders to be responsible and keep their passports safe.”
Yet the department’s own examination suggests that responsibility is only part of the story.
Some passports really are lost. Some are stolen or damaged. Others, according to officials, remain in the hands of agencies or employers their owners can no longer reach.
And some become entangled in the much murkier world of irregular migration.
Together, they have produced an extraordinary statistic: around 600 Bangladeshi passports reported “lost” every day.
